title: Fluid leak under the car
h1: What is leaking under my car?
metaDesc: Puddle under your car? Use its color, feel and location to tell oil, coolant, transmission, brake fluid or A/C water apart, and see how urgent it is.
synonyms: what is leaking from my car
intro: Most leaks can be identified by color, feel and where the puddle is. Some are harmless, like water from the air conditioning, while a brake or fuel leak means the car shouldn't be driven. Start with the safety question below, then we'll help you name the fluid.
safety: If the brake pedal feels soft or sinks, don't drive the car.
If you smell gasoline or see fuel dripping, don't start the car and keep sparks and flames away.
If the temperature gauge is in the red or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
Clean up coolant puddles right away. Coolant is poisonous, and its sweet smell attracts pets and children.

q_urgent.q: First, are any of these happening?

opts.a: The brake pedal feels soft or sinks, or the red BRAKE light is on
I smell gasoline, or the fluid smells like gas
The temperature gauge is high, there's steam, or a temperature warning is on
The oil pressure light (an oil can symbol) is on

q_color.help: Dab some onto a white paper towel or slide white cardboard under the drip. Colors are much easier to see on white. Also rub a drop between your fingers to feel whether it's watery or slick.

opts.a: Clear and watery, with no smell
Light brown to black, and slippery
Green, orange, pink or yellow, watery, with a sweet smell
Clear to yellowish or light brown, slick, near a wheel
Blue, thin, smells like window cleaner

q_location.q: Where is the spot under the car?
q_location.help: Imagine the car parked over it. Where the drip lands usually points to the part that's leaking.

opts.a: At the front, under the engine
Front passenger side, below where your feet would be
Under the middle of the car
Right next to one of the wheels
Toward the back of the car

result.title: Possible brake fluid leak. Don't drive the car
result.now: Don't drive it. Have the car towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual). A mechanic who comes to you can also inspect the brakes.
if: If the brake pedal feels firm and the brake fluid reservoir is full, the fluid may be something else. Still have a technician confirm before you use the car.
If the car is already moving and the pedal sinks, pump the brakes, use the parking brake gently and steer to a safe stop.

If the brake fluid reservoir is low but you can't find a leak, still don't drive it. Fluid can leak where you can't see it, or the level can drop as pads wear. A shop should check before you top up and go.
result.why: Brake fluid is what makes the brakes work. A leak lets fluid out and air in, and the pedal can sink to the floor with little warning. Brake fluid is clear to yellowish or brown, feels slick, and often shows up near a wheel or under the driver's side of the engine bay.

causes.name: Leaking brake caliper or wheel cylinder
causes.clues: The inside of a wheel or tire looks wet or oily.

causes.name: Rusted or damaged brake line or hose
causes.clues: Drips along the underside of the car, often on older cars in salty-winter areas.

causes.name: Leaking master cylinder
causes.clues: Wetness under the hood on the driver's side near the windshield, or a pedal that slowly sinks.

you: With the engine off, look at the brake fluid reservoir under the hood and see whether it's below the MIN mark.
Without moving the car, check whether the inside of any wheel or tire looks wet.
shop: Brake fluid level and condition check
Brake line, hose and caliper inspection

result.title: A possible fuel leak is a fire risk
result.now: Don't start the car. Keep sparks, flames and cigarettes away, and have it towed to a shop.
if: If fuel is pouring or pooling, move everyone away from the car and call the fire department.
If the smell only happens right after filling up and fades quickly, the gas cap may not be sealing. Have a technician confirm there's no leak.
result.why: Gasoline is thin, evaporates quickly and has a strong smell. A leak near a hot exhaust or a spark can start a fire, so the car shouldn't run until the leak is found and fixed.

causes.name: Leaking fuel line or hose
causes.clues: Drips along the underside of the car, between the front and back.

causes.name: Leaking fuel tank or filler neck
causes.clues: Smell or drips near the back of the car, often worse after filling up.

causes.name: Leaking fuel injector seal or fuel rail
causes.clues: The smell is strongest under the hood.

you: From a safe distance, note where the drip or smell is strongest.

result.title: Coolant may be leaking and the engine may be overheating
result.now: Turn the engine off as soon as it's safe. Don't open the radiator or coolant cap while it's hot. Have the car towed or call roadside assistance (your insurer, a motor club, or the number in your owner's manual).
if: If you're stuck in traffic and can't pull over yet, turn the heater to full hot with the fan on high. It pulls some heat away from the engine.
If steam is pouring from under the hood, stay back and let it cool before opening anything.
If the oil pressure light comes on, or you hear knocking, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and don't restart it.
result.why: Running an overheating engine can warp or crack major parts within minutes. Coolant is the green, orange, pink or yellow sweet-smelling fluid, and losing it is one of the most common reasons engines overheat.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or coolant hose
causes.clues: Drips at the front of the car, or crusty residue at hose ends.

causes.name: Failing water pump
causes.clues: Drips below the front of the engine near the belts.

causes.name: Head gasket leak
causes.clues: White exhaust smoke with a sweet smell, or coolant disappearing faster than the drip explains.
causes.against: Less likely if you can see an obvious external leak.

you: Once the engine is fully cool, check the coolant overflow tank level.
shop: Radiator, hose and water pump inspection
Combustion gas test if no outside leak is found

result.title: The engine may be dangerously low on oil
result.now: If you're driving, pull over when it's safe. Turn the engine off and leave it off. After a few minutes, check the dipstick. If it's low, add the oil type listed in your owner's manual. If you can't, have it towed.
if: If the light stays on after the level is correct, or you hear ticking or knocking, don't run the engine. Have it towed.
If oil is pouring out, don't refill and restart. Have it towed.
Even if the light goes out after topping up, a leak big enough to leave a puddle can drain the oil again quickly. Have the leak checked before driving any distance.
result.why: The oil pressure light means oil isn't reaching the engine with enough pressure to protect it. Running even briefly like that can ruin the engine. A leak big enough to leave a puddle can drain the oil quickly.

causes.name: Large leak from the drain plug, oil filter or oil pan
causes.clues: A recent oil change, or a fresh puddle that keeps growing.

causes.name: Very low oil level from a slow leak or oil burning
causes.clues: Oil hasn't been checked in a while, or blue smoke from the exhaust.

causes.name: Failing oil pump or pressure sensor
causes.clues: The light stays on even though the oil level is full. A shop will usually measure the real oil pressure with a gauge before replacing the sensor or pump.

you: Check the oil level with the engine off and the car on level ground.
If the oil was just changed, look for a loose drain plug or oil filter.

result.title: Possibly just water from the air conditioning
result.now: Rub a drop between your fingers. If it's clear, odorless and not slippery, and you've been using the A/C or defroster, it's most likely normal A/C condensation, which doesn't need a repair.
if: If it feels slippery, smells sweet or has any color, it isn't plain water. Go back and pick the color instead.
If water is collecting on the passenger-side floor inside the car, the A/C drain may be blocked. Book a check.
result.why: The A/C pulls moisture out of the cabin air and drains it under the car, usually near the front passenger side. On hot, humid days it can leave a surprisingly large puddle. This is a normal part of how A/C works.

causes.name: Normal A/C condensation
causes.clues: Hot or humid weather, and the A/C or defroster was on.

causes.name: Water from the exhaust
causes.clues: Drips from the tailpipe, mostly on cold starts.

causes.name: Coolant leak
causes.clues: A faint sweet smell, a slick feel, or the coolant tank level dropping.
causes.against: Plain A/C water has no smell and isn't slick.

you: Check that the puddle is near the front passenger side.
Check the coolant overflow tank level when the engine is cold.
shop: A/C drain inspection if water gets inside the car

result.title: Likely an engine oil leak
result.now: Check the oil level on the dipstick and top up if needed. Book a check to find the source when convenient.
if: If the oil is below the low mark, or the spot is bigger than your hand after one night, get it checked within a few days.

If you see smoke or smell burning oil from under the hood, pull over, turn the engine off and let it cool. Oil may be dripping onto the hot exhaust, which can be a fire risk. Have it checked before driving further.
If the oil pressure light comes on, or you hear ticking or knocking, pull over as soon as it's safe and turn the engine off right away.
result.why: Engine oil is light brown when fresh, dark brown or black when used, and feels slippery. Many oil leaks are slow seeps from gaskets that harden with age and heat. The main risks are running low and oil dripping onto hot parts, so keep an eye on the level.

causes.name: Oil pan gasket or drain plug
causes.clues: Drips at the bottom of the engine, especially after a recent oil change.

causes.name: Valve cover gasket
causes.clues: Oil on the top or sides of the engine, or a burning-oil smell after driving.

causes.name: Crankshaft seal at the front or rear of the engine
causes.clues: Drips where the engine meets the transmission, or at the front behind the belts.

you: Check the oil level with the car on level ground and the engine off.
Slide cardboard under the engine overnight to see how much drips and from where.
With a flashlight and the engine off, look for wet, oily areas on the engine.
shop: Oil leak inspection, with dye if needed

result.title: Possibly transmission fluid or power steering fluid
result.now: Book a check within the next few days. If your car has a transmission dipstick or a see-through power steering reservoir, check those levels.
if: If the transmission slips, shifts hard or is slow to go into gear, stop driving it and have it towed.
If the steering suddenly gets heavy or hard to turn, pull over when it's safe and don't drive it until it's checked.
If it smells like gasoline, don't start the car. Keep sparks and flames away and have it towed.
If the fluid is thin, clear to yellowish and slick, or the brake pedal feels different, it may be brake fluid. Don't drive the car until it's checked.
result.why: Red or pink oily fluid is often automatic transmission fluid, and some power steering systems use it too. Transmission leaks tend to drip under the middle of the car, power steering leaks near the front. Running either system low can damage it.

causes.name: Transmission pan gasket, cooler line or seal
causes.clues: A spot under the middle or front of the car, or shifting that has changed.

causes.name: Power steering hose or pump
causes.clues: A spot near the front, or a whine when turning the wheel.
causes.against: Many newer cars have electric power steering with no fluid at all.

causes.name: Pink coolant
causes.clues: A sweet smell and a watery feel.
causes.against: Transmission and power steering fluid feel oily, not watery.

you: Note whether the spot is under the middle or the front of the car.
Rub a drop between your fingers: oily means transmission or power steering fluid, watery and sweet means coolant.
Check fluid levels where your owner's manual shows a dipstick or reservoir.
shop: Transmission and power steering leak inspection

result.title: Possibly a coolant (antifreeze) leak
result.now: With the engine cold, check the coolant overflow tank and top it up with the type in your owner's manual. Get the leak checked within a few days and watch the temperature gauge.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
If it's a steady drip, or the tank is low again within a day or two, have it towed rather than risk overheating.
If you see white smoke from the exhaust with a sweet smell, or the coolant keeps disappearing with no drip, mention it to the shop and avoid driving until it's checked.
result.why: Coolant is usually green, orange, pink or yellow, feels watery and smells sweet. Small leaks tend to grow, and running low on coolant leads to overheating, which can badly damage the engine.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or coolant hose
causes.clues: Drips at the front of the car, or crusty, colored residue at hose ends.

causes.name: Leaking water pump
causes.clues: Drips below the front of the engine near the belts.

causes.name: Leaking heater core
causes.clues: A sweet smell inside the car, a damp passenger floor, or windows that fog up.
causes.against: Usually leaks inside the car rather than underneath it.

you: Check the coolant overflow tank level when the engine is cold.
Look for crusty residue around the radiator and hose ends.
Wipe up the puddle so pets can't drink it.
shop: Radiator, hose and water pump inspection

result.title: Possibly windshield washer fluid
result.now: Fill the washer fluid reservoir and watch for drips. A cracked tank or a loose hose is a common cause.
if: If it smells sweet or the coolant tank is also dropping, it may be coolant. Get it checked within a few days.
If the washers don't spray, the pump or a hose is probably where it's leaking.
result.why: Washer fluid is usually blue, thin like water, and smells like window cleaner. A washer leak won't harm the car, but you need working washers to see clearly in bad weather.

causes.name: Cracked washer fluid reservoir
causes.clues: The tank empties within days without using the washers.

causes.name: Loose or split washer hose
causes.clues: Drips mostly after using the washers.

causes.name: Coolant
causes.clues: A sweet smell, or the coolant tank is dropping too.
causes.against: Washer fluid smells like window cleaner, not sweet.

you: Fill the reservoir and look under it for drips.
Smell the fluid: window cleaner means washer fluid, sweet means coolant.
shop: Washer reservoir, pump and hose inspection

result.title: Fluid under the engine is often oil or coolant
result.now: With the engine cold and off, check the oil dipstick, the coolant overflow tank and the brake fluid reservoir. Whichever is low may be the leak. Book a check to confirm.
if: If either level is below the low mark, top it up and get it checked within a few days.
If the temperature gauge rises or the oil pressure light comes on, pull over and turn the engine off.
If the brake fluid reservoir is below the MIN mark, don't drive the car until it's inspected, even if you can't see where it's leaking.
If you see smoke or smell burning from under the hood, pull over as soon as it's safe, turn the engine off and let it cool before doing anything else.
result.why: The engine sits at the front of most cars, and the two fluids it holds the most of are oil and coolant. Checking both levels is the fastest way to tell which one you're losing.

causes.name: Engine oil leak
causes.clues: Brown or black, slippery, and the oil level is dropping.

causes.name: Coolant leak
causes.clues: Watery, sweet-smelling, and the coolant tank is dropping.

causes.name: Power steering fluid leak
causes.clues: Red or amber and oily, with a whine when turning.
causes.against: Many newer cars use electric steering with no fluid.

you: Check the oil level, the coolant overflow tank and the brake fluid reservoir.
Slide white cardboard under the engine overnight to see the color.

result.title: A drip toward the back is often exhaust water, axle oil or fuel
result.now: If it's clear water dripping from the tailpipe, that's usually normal condensation. Otherwise, note its color and smell and book a check when convenient.
if: If it smells like gasoline, don't start the car. Have it towed.
If it's slick and right next to a rear wheel, it may be brake fluid. Don't drive the car until it's checked.
If it's thick oil with a strong, sulfur-like smell near the middle of the rear axle, get it checked within a few days.
result.why: Exhaust makes water as it runs, and it often drips from the tailpipe on cold starts. Rear-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive cars also have gear oil in the rear axle. The fuel tank sits at the back too, so smell is an important clue.

causes.name: Exhaust condensation
causes.clues: Clear water from the tailpipe, mostly on cold mornings or short trips.

causes.name: Rear axle (differential) oil leak
causes.clues: Thick, dark oil with a strong smell, on a rear-wheel or all-wheel-drive car.

causes.name: Fuel tank or fuel line leak
causes.clues: A gasoline smell.

causes.name: Rear brake leak
causes.clues: Slick fluid on the inside of a rear wheel.

you: Note whether the drip comes from the tailpipe or from under the car.
Smell the fluid from a safe distance.
shop: Rear axle seal and cover check

result.title: Collect a sample so you or a shop can identify the leak
result.now: Slide a large piece of white cardboard under the car overnight. In the morning, note the color, where it dripped and how big the spot is, then book a check.
if: If the brake pedal feels soft or the brake light is on, don't drive the car.
If you smell gasoline, don't start the car and keep flames away.
If a warning light comes on, follow what that light means first.
If the temperature gauge is high or you see steam, pull over and turn the engine off.
result.why: Color, feel and location together identify nearly every leak. A clean white surface makes the color obvious, and where the spot lands points to the part that's leaking.

causes.name: Engine oil
causes.clues: Brown or black and slippery, under the engine.

causes.name: Coolant
causes.clues: Green, orange, pink or yellow, watery and sweet.

causes.name: A/C water
causes.clues: Clear and odorless, near the front passenger side.

you: Take a photo of the spot on the cardboard to show the shop.
Check the oil, coolant and brake fluid levels with the engine off. If the brake fluid is below MIN, don't drive the car until it's inspected.
